option_1.en: Its kinetic energy grows in direct proportion to the distance it has fallen

option_2.en: Its kinetic energy equals its potential energy at half the original height

option_3.en: Its kinetic energy grows in direct proportion to the time it has fallen

option_4.en: Its total mechanical energy is the same at every point of the fall

question.en: For a body falling freely from rest under gravity, which statement is NOT correct?

solution_text.en:
Answer: Option 3 — Its kinetic energy grows in direct proportion to the time it has fallen

In free fall the speed grows as v = gt, so the kinetic energy 1/2 mv² = 1/2 mg²t² grows with the square of the time, not in direct proportion to it.

Against distance the growth is linear: after falling x, the body has lost mgx of potential energy and gained exactly mgx of kinetic energy. At half the height the two are equal (mgh/2 each), and the total stays mgh throughout.

Revision note — conservation and transformation of energy

  • Law of conservation of energy: energy is neither created nor destroyed, only changed in form; the total energy of an isolated system is constant.
  • For a body dropped from height h: at the top PE = mgh, KE = 0; at the ground KE = mgh, PE = 0; the landing speed is v = (2gh)^(1/2).
  • At any height y: PE = mgy and KE = mg(h - y), and their sum is always mgh.
  • KE = 1/2 mv² — doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times, tripling it nine times.
  • Gravitational PE = mgh depends only on the vertical height, not on the path taken.
  • The SI unit of work and energy is the joule (1 J = 1 N m); power is measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s).
  • 1 kilowatt-hour = 3.6 x 10^6 joules; 1 horsepower = 746 watts.
  • Everyday transformations: dynamo (mechanical to electrical), electric motor (electrical to mechanical), photosynthesis (light to chemical), loudspeaker (electrical to sound).

question.en:
Consider the following statements about the order of rights in Part III.

I. The Right against Exploitation comes immediately after the Right to Freedom.

II. Cultural and Educational Rights are placed before the Right to Freedom of Religion.

III. The Right to Constitutional Remedies is the last of the six Fundamental Rights.

Which of the above statements are correct?

solution_text.en:
Answer: Option 2 — I and III only

Part III lists the rights in this order: Right to Equality (Articles 14-18), Right to Freedom (19-22), Right against Exploitation (23-24), Right to Freedom of Religion (25-28), Cultural and Educational Rights (29-30) and Right to Constitutional Remedies (32).

Statement II reverses the real sequence — religion comes before the cultural and educational rights. Statements I and III match the text of the Constitution.

Revision note — Fundamental Rights, Part III (Articles 12-35)

  • Part III is modelled on the Bill of Rights of the United States Constitution and is called the Magna Carta of India.
  • There were originally seven rights; the Right to Property was removed by the 44th Amendment, 1978, and is now a legal right under Article 300A.
  • Article 12 defines 'the State'; Article 13 voids laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights and is the basis of judicial review.
  • 14 equality before law, 15 no discrimination, 16 equality of opportunity in public employment, 17 abolition of untouchability, 18 abolition of titles.
  • 19 six freedoms, 20 protection in respect of conviction, 21 life and personal liberty, 21A free education for ages 6-14 (86th Amendment, 2002), 22 protection against arrest.
  • 23 bans traffic in human beings and forced labour; 24 bans employment of children below 14 in factories and mines.
  • 25-28 freedom of religion; 29-30 cultural and educational rights of minorities.
  • Article 32, called by Ambedkar the heart and soul of the Constitution, provides the five writs — habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto.

Also asked from this topic: the order in which the Fundamental Rights appear in the Constitution (SSC Stenographer 2025), the Article that confers the right to constitutional remedies (SSC CGL Tier-1 2025), and the Article declaring laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void (Delhi Police Constable (Exe) 2025-26).

question.en: The Supreme Court's 2025 opinion on timelines for assent to State Bills came under which Article?

solution_text.en:
Answer: Option 1 — Article 143

Under Article 143 the President may refer to the Supreme Court any question of law or fact of public importance for its advisory opinion, and that opinion is not binding on the President.

The Presidential Reference of 2025 asked whether courts may fix time limits for a Governor (Article 200) and the President (Article 201) to act on Bills. In its opinion the Court held that no judicially enforceable timeline can be imposed and that a Bill cannot be given deemed assent.

Revision note — the President's powers and Article 143

  • Article 143(1) covers any question of law or fact of public importance — the Court may decline to answer; under 143(2), on pre-Constitution treaties, it must report its opinion.
  • Well-known references include Delhi Laws Act (1951), Kerala Education Bill (1958), Berubari Union (1960), Presidential Poll (1974), Cauvery (1992) and Ayodhya (1993).
  • Legislative powers of the President: summoning, proroguing and dissolving under Article 85, addressing Parliament under Article 87 and promulgating ordinances under Article 123.
  • Veto powers available: absolute, suspensive and pocket — there is no qualified veto for the Indian President.
  • A Money Bill needs the President's prior recommendation and cannot be returned to the House for reconsideration.
  • Article 72 gives the pardoning power — pardon, commutation, remission, respite and reprieve.
  • Under Article 200 a Governor may assent, withhold assent, return a Bill or reserve it for the President; under Article 201 the President may assent or withhold assent.
  • The President is elected by an electoral college of elected MPs and elected MLAs through proportional representation with a single transferable vote, and is removed by impeachment under Article 61.

solution_text.en:
Answer: Option 4 — The Sense of an Ending — Julian Barnes

Julian Barnes won the Booker Prize in 2011 for The Sense of an Ending. The other three pairs move a real winner to the wrong book: The Remains of the Day (1989) is by Kazuo Ishiguro, Midnight's Children (1981) by Salman Rushdie and The God of Small Things (1997) by Arundhati Roy.

Kazuo Ishiguro, born in Nagasaki and settled in Britain, also won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2017.

Revision note — the Booker Prize

  • Instituted in 1969 in the United Kingdom; called the Man Booker Prize between 2002 and 2019; awarded for a novel written in English and published in the UK or Ireland.
  • From 2014 writers of any nationality are eligible, not only those of the Commonwealth and Ireland.
  • The separate International Booker Prize honours a translated work, and its money is shared equally by the author and the translator.
  • Geetanjali Shree won the International Booker in 2022 for Tomb of Sand (Ret Samadhi), translated by Daisy Rockwell — the first Hindi work to win it.
  • Indian and Indian-origin Booker winners: V. S. Naipaul (1971), Salman Rushdie (1981), Arundhati Roy (1997), Kiran Desai (2006) and Aravind Adiga (2008).
  • Midnight's Children also won the Booker of Bookers.
  • Jhumpa Lahiri won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction (2000) for Interpreter of Maladies — a different award altogether.
  • Kiran Desai is the daughter of the novelist Anita Desai; her winning book was The Inheritance of Loss.

question.en:
Consider the following statements about Kathakali.

I. It is a classical dance-drama of Kerala, performed traditionally by men.

II. Its stories are drawn mainly from the Ramayana and the Mahabharata.

III. Its performers wear the chutti, a frame built up on the face.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

solution_text.en:
Answer: Option 3 — I, II and III

Kathakali — from katha, a story, and kali, play — is the dance-drama of Kerala, performed traditionally through the night by male actor-dancers, who take the female roles as well.

Its repertoire, the attakatha, comes from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Puranas, and its make-up builds a stiff white frame called the chutti around the face, with colour codes such as pacha (green) for noble characters and kathi for anti-heroes.

Revision note — classical dances of India

  • The Sangeet Natak Akademi recognises eight classical dances: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam and Sattriya.
  • Kerala contributes two of them — Kathakali and Mohiniyattam, the solo 'dance of the enchantress' performed by women.
  • Kathakali's accompaniment uses the chenda and maddalam drums, the chengila gong and sopanam singing.
  • All eight trace their grammar to Bharata's Natya Shastra, whose four abhinayas are angika, vachika, aharya and satvika.
  • Kathak is the principal classical dance of North India, with the Lucknow, Jaipur and Banaras gharanas.
  • Sattriya of Assam grew in the sattras founded by Srimanta Sankardeva and was recognised as classical in 2000.
  • Kuchipudi of Andhra Pradesh is known for the tarangam, danced on the rim of a brass plate.
  • Chhau, Yakshagana and Therukoothu are folk or semi-classical forms, outside the classical eight.
